source.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
source.authors: Tom McGrath; Matthew Rahtz; János Kramár; Vladimir Mikulik; S. Legg

page_placements.theme: Self-repair after ablation is common but partial, and its size varies with model, data and training
MLP layers also suppress already-promoted or earlier tokens, depending on upstream attention

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies layer-level self-repair in Chinchilla 7B, but does not test L10H7, copy suppression, calibration, or the specific upstream-copier ablation mechanism in the claim versions. Its mention of GPT-2 Small backup heads is a citation to other work, not a result of this study.
record.gate_note: The authors report their own layer-ablation and compensation results, recorded below as findings about self-repair that fit none of the specified versions. They cite GPT-2 Small backup-head results from Wang et al. (2022), but those cited results are not recorded as this study's results. The paper says that analysis at individual-head or direction level is a natural next step.
record.test_reason: The study ablates whole attention and MLP layers in Chinchilla 7B on Counterfact factual-recall prompts. It measures layer-level self-repair: downstream attention compensation (the Hydra effect) and attenuated late-MLP erasure. It never analyses individual heads, copy suppression, GPT-2 small L10H7, QK/OV circuits, calibration, or copy suppression's share of self-repair. Its results therefore bear on no version. It predates the original source and does not cite it. Its GPT-2 Small 'backup heads' mention cites Wang et al. (2022) and is not this study's result.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that ablating an attention layer makes another attention layer compensate (the Hydra effect). Late MLPs act as erasure/negative feedback on the top token, and this is attenuated under ablation. Together these responses are roughly linear and restore about 70% of the logit reduction at middle layers. The record omits that the authors also argue this disproves dropout as the cause of self-repair, since Chinchilla 7B was trained without dropout.
record.recipe_differences: This study uses resample ablations and layer-level logit-effect analysis in Chinchilla 7B on Counterfact prompts. It does not use the head-level QK/OV circuit analysis or copy-suppression measurements described by the original claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The balance between attention and MLP responses changes with network depth: attention responses matter more in early layers, while MLP responses become more predictive at layer 22 and account for almost all of the response at layer 23.

fits_no_version.finding: In Chinchilla 7B on 1,209 Counterfact prompts, ablating an attention layer makes downstream layers compensate. At layer 23 compensation explains 92% of variance in downstream ΔDE. Regression slopes are below 1 past layer 13. At middle layers compensation restores about 70% of the logit reduction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer-level ablations in large LMs elicit partial, approximately linear downstream compensation (Hydra effect plus reduced MLP erasure) that does not fully restore the output.

fits_no_version.finding: Late-layer 'erasure' MLPs reduce the maximum-likelihood token's logit, and this reduction shrinks when upstream attention layers promoting the token are ablated. By layers 22–23, the MLP response dominates the compensation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Late MLP layers act as negative feedback on the top token, and their attenuation after upstream ablation is a major source of self-repair. This is an MLP analogue of, but distinct from, head-level copy suppression.

record.problems: The evidence is layer-level and limited to factual-recall prompts from Counterfact; the authors note that finer-grained analysis of individual heads or directions remains to be done. Several results are presented in figures without numerical values in the text, and the paper describes some initial examples as largely anecdotal.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version results were reported. Figure-only layer-by-layer values are not entered separately where the text does not state their values.

untested.parts: All: no GPT-2 small, no L10H7, no head-level role analysis across the training distribution.
All: no QK/OV circuit analysis and no loss-share measurement.
All: no calibration measurement. 'Recalibration' by erasure heads is only listed as an open question.
No ablation of an upstream copier and no measurement of reduced copy suppression. The compensation measured is layer-level attention and MLP response on factual recall.
All: no negative name movers, no comparison of negative heads across models or sizes.
Self-repair sources are split only into downstream attention versus MLP layers. Copy suppression and LayerNorm rescaling are not separated, so copy suppression's share is not estimated.

record.verdict_notes: Relevant background for V4/V6, because it documents non-copy-suppression self-repair sources (downstream attention, erasure MLPs). But it is layer-level, in a different model and task, and never isolates copy suppression, so no verdicts are given. The record's relation, tranche and version statuses are kept.

versions.untested_parts: No analysis of GPT-2 small L10H7, token copying, or whether a head has one main role across the training distribution.
No QK or OV circuit analysis of L10H7 and no measurement of copy suppression's share of loss.
No test of copy suppression or calibration.
The study measures layer-level compensation after layer ablations, but does not ablate an upstream copier or test whether reduced copy suppression partly compensates.
No test of negative name movers, copy suppression in other models or sizes, or whether these are the same role.
The study reports other layer-level responses to ablation, but does not compare them with copy suppression or estimate copy suppression's share of self-repair across the distribution.

rows.subject: Chinchilla 7B
rows.operation_detail: Resample-ablated attention layers and measured downstream compensatory effects.
rows.measure: Variance in downstream direct-effect changes explained by compensatory effects
rows.note: The paper identifies layer 23 as the high point of compensation; the reported percentage concerns variance explained, not a fraction of loss or copy suppression.
rows.check: The text attributes the 92% of variance in downstream ΔDE to 'the Hydra effect' at layer 23. Elsewhere it says the response at layer 23 occurs almost entirely in erasure MLPs. The measure label should read 'compensatory effect (attention + MLP)', not Hydra attention alone.

rows.subject: Chinchilla 7B
rows.operation_detail: Resample-ablated layers and compared direct effects with downstream compensatory response.
rows.measure: Slope of linear regression between direct effect and compensatory response
rows.baseline: Full restoration would correspond to a slope of 1
rows.value: Less than one at all layers past layer 13
rows.note: The authors state that this means ablations retain a nonzero total effect, reduced by the Hydra effect and MLP responses.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, paragraph on incomplete restoration; Figure 7.

rows.subject: Chinchilla 7B
rows.operation_detail: Ablated middle layers and measured restoration of token logits by downstream Hydra and MLP responses.
rows.measure: Reduction in token logits restored by the Hydra effect and MLP responses
rows.note: This is the authors' aggregate summary for middle layers; it is not a measurement of copy suppression.
rows.check: Comes from the conclusion's aggregate summary (about 70% restored at middle layers), not a separately reported table value. Keep it, but mark it as an author summary of Figure 7 slopes.

rows.subject: Chinchilla 7B
rows.operation_detail: Ablated early layers and measured their direct and total effects.
rows.measure: Direct effects compared with total effects
rows.value: Large total effects but almost no direct effect
rows.note: The paper describes this as an early-layer pattern; it does not name a numeric layer range here.

rows.subject: Chinchilla 7B
rows.operation_detail: Ablated late layers and measured their direct effects.
rows.value: Non-negligible direct effect; few downstream layers available for an effect
rows.note: The authors contrast this pattern with early-layer ablations.

rows.subject: Chinchilla 7B
rows.operation_detail: Ablated attention layers and compared downstream attention and MLP responses.
rows.measure: Relative predictive contribution of downstream MLP and attention responses
rows.value: The MLP response was considerably more predictive
rows.note: The paper describes a shift toward MLP responses with depth.

rows.subject: Chinchilla 7B
rows.operation_detail: Ablated attention layers and compared downstream MLP and attention responses.
rows.measure: Share of the response occurring in erasure MLPs
rows.note: The authors characterize these late MLPs as erasure MLPs.

relation.reason: Provides related self-repair findings without testing or using the specified copy-suppression mechanism.

tranche.reason: Measures layer-level self-repair during factual recall, without identifying copy suppression or measuring its share of self-repair across the distribution.

source_check.notes: The 92% measures variance explained, not restoration; the paper attributes almost all layer 23 response to erasure MLPs despite also using Hydra terminology. Approximately 70% restoration is the authors' conclusion summary; the V4/V6 connections are analogies, not tests.
